title: Design a news feed (Twitter/Instagram)
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, API, estimates, fan-out push/pull/hybrid, feed storage, ranking, counters, deletes.

Scope: requirements, API, estimates, fan-out push/pull/hybrid, feed storage, ranking, counters, deletes.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A news feed shows each user a stream of posts from the people they follow, newest and most relevant first. Twitter/X home timeline, Instagram feed, Facebook News Feed, LinkedIn feed. The famous trick is deciding whether to do the work when someone posts (fan-out on write) or when someone reads (fan-out on read). This note is the full interview version of the Chirp stage in the Master scaling track (stage 6, where a hybrid timeline appears); read that for how it evolves with scale.

Functional requirements

  • Post (text, images, video) and follow/unfollow.
  • Home feed: posts from followees, reverse-chronological or ranked, infinitely scrollable.
  • Likes, comments, reposts; user profile timeline (a user's own posts).
  • Notifications of new activity (optional).

Non-functional requirements

  • Feed load under 200 ms p99 (the main screen of the product).
  • Posting feels instant; followers may see it a few seconds later (eventual consistency is fine).
  • Read-heavy: 100 to 1000 feed reads per post.
  • Highly available; stale feed is acceptable, empty feed is not.
  • Handles celebrities (100M followers) and normal users (200 followers) in one system.

Decision gravity. The push versus pull decision (and the hybrid) shapes data model, cost and latency for years. Wrong choice shows as either massive write amplification (push for celebrities) or slow reads (pull for everyone). Moving later is a major migration.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper: print and deliver a personalised copy to each subscriber's door (push), or have subscribers visit the kiosk and pick articles when they want (pull).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping into ranking ML before stating the fan-out strategy.
  • Ignoring the celebrity case.
  • Not asking: chronological or ranked? How many followees on average?

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/posts
Idempotency-Key: 6d2e-...
{ "text": "hello world", "mediaIds": ["m_81"], "replyTo": null }
201 { "postId": "1853740192837465088", "createdAt": "2026-11-09T10:15:00Z" }

POST /v1/users/u_42/follow        -> 204 (idempotent)
DELETE /v1/users/u_42/follow      -> 204
GET /v1/feed/home?cursor=1853740192837465088&limit=20
200 { "items": [ { "postId":"...", "author":{"id":"u_7","name":"Asha"}, "text":"...",
                   "media":[...], "counts":{"likes":341,"replies":12}, "likedByMe":false } ],
      "nextCursor": "1853740192837400000" }

GET /v1/users/u_7/posts?cursor=...&limit=20      // profile timeline
POST /v1/posts/{id}/like        -> 204 (idempotent)

Pagination is cursor-based using the post id (time-sortable), never OFFSET, because new posts shift offsets and duplicate or skip items. Post ids are Snowflake-style 64-bit integers (timestamp in the high bits) so they sort by time and carry no coordination cost.

Industry example. Twitter's Snowflake id generator (41 bits time, 10 bits machine, 12 bits sequence); Instagram built a similar scheme inside Postgres embedding shard id.

Everyday analogy. A bookmark in the stack of papers: "continue after this one", unaffected by new papers added on top.

Common interview traps.

  • Offset pagination (duplicates and skips as the feed moves).
  • Returning full post bodies for each feed item from the feed store instead of hydrating.
  • Non-idempotent like/follow endpoints.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 300M DAU, each opens the feed 10 times/day, posts 0.5/day on average, follows 200 users, 20% of users post per day.

Quantity Calculation Result
Posts 300M x 0.5 150M/day, 1,700/s avg, peak ~5,000/s
Feed reads 300M x 10 / 86,400 35,000/s avg, peak ~100,000/s
Read:write 35,000 / 1,700 ~20:1 on requests (higher once refresh is counted)
Fan-out on write 150M posts x 200 followers avg 30B feed inserts/day = 350,000/s avg
Feed cache size 300M users x 800 post ids x 8 B ~2 TB (ids only)
Post storage 150M x 1 KB (text+metadata) 150 GB/day, ~55 TB/year (media separate, in object storage)
Celebrity post 100M followers x 1 post 100M inserts for one post

What this tells you. Pushing to 200 followers on average is fine (350k cheap in-memory inserts per second across a cluster); the celebrity case (100M inserts for one tweet) breaks it. Keeping only ids (8 B) in the feed cache makes 2 TB feasible across 30 to 60 Redis nodes at 64 GB each. Media is the real storage and bandwidth cost: serve from a CDN.

Everyday analogy. Delivering 200 newspapers is a normal morning; delivering 100 million at once for a single edition needs a different plan.

Common interview traps.

  • Using average followers and forgetting the long tail.
  • Storing full post JSON in each follower's feed (storage explosion).
  • Not separating media from text storage.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Post service: validates, assigns id, writes to the Posts DB (sharded by author or post id), emits post.created to Kafka (outbox).
  • Social graph service: followers(userId) and following(userId) lists; adjacency in a sharded store (MySQL like Facebook TAO, or Redis/Cassandra); cached.
  • Fan-out workers: consume post.created, look up followers, insert the post id into each follower's feed list.
  • Feed cache: per user Redis sorted set or list of (postId) limited to the latest 500 to 800.
  • Feed service: reads ids from the cache, merges in celebrity posts (pull), hydrates posts (batched MGET), applies ranking and filters (blocked, muted), returns a page.
  • Counters (likes, replies): separate high-throughput counter store; eventually consistent.

Industry examples. Twitter's 2012 timeline architecture: home timelines in Redis (about 800 entries), fan-out on write, with celebrities handled separately; Instagram: Cassandra/Postgres plus caching, move to ranked feed; Facebook: ranked pull-based aggregation of many sources (leaf servers), famously more compute on read because the ranking is personalised.

Decision gravity. Store ids only and hydrate at read time. It decouples the feed from post edits and deletes (the post store is the single source of truth), at the cost of an extra batched read. Reversible and cheap.

Everyday analogy. The feed holds a list of article numbers; the printing office hands you the actual article when you open the paper.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying the post body into every feed (edits and deletes become impossible).
  • One synchronous fan-out inside the post request.
  • Using SQL joins posts JOIN follows at read time at this scale.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read vs hybrid

Fan-out on read (pull). When Asha opens the feed: get her followees (200), fetch recent posts of each (200 queries or one multi-get), merge by time, take top 20. Write is trivial; read is expensive (200 lookups and a merge per open, 100k opens/s = 20M lookups/s).

Fan-out on write (push). When a post is created: look up the author's followers, insert the post id into each follower's feed list. Read is one Redis call (ZREVRANGE). Write amplification equals the follower count.

Hybrid (what Twitter and Instagram settled on). Push for normal authors; for authors above a threshold (for example 100k to 1M followers), do not push. At read time, take the user's precomputed feed (pushed items) and merge in recent posts from the few celebrities that user follows (pull from the celebrity's own timeline, cached heavily).

# Feed read (hybrid)
def home_feed(user, cursor, n=20):
    ids = redis.zrevrangebyscore(f"feed:{user}", cursor, "-inf", start=0, num=n+20)
    for c in celebrity_followees(user):                       # usually under 20
        ids += timeline_cache.recent(c, since=cursor, limit=n)
    ids = sorted(set(ids), reverse=True)[:n]                  # snowflake ids sort by time
    return hydrate(ids)

Additional tricks:

  • Active-user-only fan-out: do not push into feeds of users inactive for 30 days (saves 30 to 50% of work); rebuild their feed lazily when they return (a pull).
  • Batching and priorities: fan-out through Kafka partitions keyed by author; paid or close-friend recipients first.
  • Backpressure: if fan-out lags, the post is still available through pull for the author's profile and the feed is simply slightly stale.

Decision gravity. The follower threshold is a policy knob (reversible per author), but the hybrid read path is a permanent architectural component. Alternative: pure pull with massive caching, which Facebook does for ranked feeds because ranking is computed per request anyway. Hybrid breaks if the pull set per user grows (following many celebrities); cap or rank which celebrities to pull.

Everyday analogy. The mail carrier delivers letters from ordinary senders to your mailbox, but a famous newsletter's issue sits in the lobby for you to pick up.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "push" without addressing celebrities, or "pull" without addressing read cost.
  • Not stating the threshold or how it's decided.
  • Merging at read time without a time-sorted id.

Feed storage and data model

Redis sorted set feed:{userId} with ZADD feed:42 <score=postId> <member=postId> and ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:42 0 -801 to cap at 800. Memory per entry about 40 to 60 B in a sorted set (use a plain list or a compact encoding for lower, since score and member are the same id; many designs use a list with LPUSH/LTRIM and the time-sorted id embedded).

Sharding: hash userId over Redis nodes (consistent hashing or Redis Cluster with 16,384 slots). Replication: 1 replica; the feed is a cache that can be rebuilt from the graph and posts, so durability is not critical; losing a node means a rebuild by pull for affected users.

Posts DB: sharded by postId or authorId. Author sharding gives cheap profile timelines but creates hot shards for celebrities; id sharding spreads writes but needs scatter for the profile page (served by a secondary index/cache). Instagram chose sharding with the shard id embedded in the 64-bit id. Posts are immutable except edits and deletes; deletes are soft (tombstone), and the hydrator drops tombstoned ids.

CREATE TABLE posts (
  post_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,         -- snowflake
  author_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  body TEXT, media JSONB, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  deleted BOOLEAN DEFAULT false);
CREATE INDEX posts_by_author ON posts (author_id, post_id DESC);

Decision gravity. Treat the feed cache as derived and rebuildable; do not pay for strong durability. The rebuild path must exist and be fast (hundreds of ms) or a node loss becomes an outage when millions of users miss at once (cache stampede, add jitter and request coalescing).

Everyday analogy. A to-read pile you can rebuild at any time from the newspaper archive.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating Redis feed as the system of record.
  • Rebuilds for millions of users at once without throttling.
  • Unbounded feed length.

Ranking and hydration

Chronological feed: sort by id. Ranked feed (Instagram, Facebook, modern X): two stages.

  1. Candidate generation: the latest 500 candidates from push + pull (+ recommended content).
  2. Ranking: a model scores each candidate (P(like), P(comment), P(dwell)) from features (author affinity, recency, post type, user history), with business rules (diversity, no 5 posts in a row from one author, filter blocked and muted users). Then top N.

Latency budget: 200 ms total: Redis ids 5 ms, hydrate posts 20 ms (batched MGET from a posts cache with 95% hit rate), features 30 ms (feature store), model 50 ms (served from a GPU/CPU model server), counters 10 ms, overhead. Precompute features offline and keep affinity scores in a feature store; cache the final ranked page for 30 to 60 s per user to survive refresh spam.

Hydration is batched: collect all ids, MGET post:{id} from Redis, fetch misses from the DB in one WHERE post_id IN (...), fill the cache. Counters (likes) are read from a separate counter service with a cached value that is a few seconds stale.

Decision gravity. Ranking is policy and highly reversible (A/B test everything), but it commits you to the infrastructure cost (feature store, model serving) and the risk of "filter bubble" and trust issues. Keep a chronological fallback path and a kill switch for the model.

Everyday analogy. An editor choosing which of the 500 stories go on the front page, balancing freshness and what each reader tends to enjoy.

Common interview traps.

  • Ranking inline with a synchronous cold call to the DB per candidate.
  • No fallback when the ranker is down.
  • Ignoring blocked and muted users in the push path (filter at read time too).

Counters, likes and hot posts

Likes arrive at high rates for viral posts (100k likes/s on one post). Counting by UPDATE posts SET likes=likes+1 row-locks a hot row. Instead:

  • Write the like event (user, post) to Kafka and a likes table (dedupe by (user, post) unique key for idempotence).
  • Maintain the counter in Redis with INCR, sharded for hot keys (split into N sub-counters, sum on read), flush periodically to the DB.
  • The displayed count is approximate for hot posts (eventually consistent), exact for "did I like it" (from the likes table/bitmap per user).

Decision gravity. Accepting approximate counters is a product decision that removes the hottest DB row in the system, reversible. Exactness is only required for the user's own state.

Industry example. Facebook TAO caches associations and counts with write-through and eventual consistency; Twitter's counters aggregate asynchronously ("Rainbird"-style, confirm names with current engineering posts).

Everyday analogy. A stadium tally clicker per gate rather than one clicker everyone fights over.

Common interview traps.

  • A single row per post counter updated in place.
  • Letting a duplicate like request increment twice.

Media, deletes and failure handling

Media goes to object storage via presigned upload; a transcoder produces renditions; the CDN serves them. Post stores only the media ids and URLs.

Deletes: soft delete in the post DB, publish post.deleted, workers remove ids from feeds lazily; the hydrator filters tombstoned posts immediately, so the user sees consistent results even if feeds still hold the id. GDPR hard delete is an async job.

Failure modes:

  • Fan-out worker lag: metric is consumer lag; scale workers; the product degrades to slightly older feeds.
  • Redis node down: replica promoted; users on the lost shard rebuilt on demand with throttling.
  • Graph service down: serve cached feed without refresh.
  • Celebrity post spike: hot post cache replicated to local caches (1 to 5 s TTL); CDN for media.

Everyday analogy. Pulling an article from the archive immediately, then slowly removing the clippings from the subscribers' piles.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard deleting and leaving ghost ids that break hydration.
  • No plan for a cold Redis after a restart.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Strategy with numbers: fan-out on write vs read vs hybrid, the celebrity threshold, write amplification (350k inserts/s).
  • Data model: ids only in the feed, Snowflake ids, cursor pagination, cap length.
  • Hydration and counters design; cache hit ratio reasoning.
  • Ranking pipeline basics and latency budget; chronological fallback.
  • Failure and skew: celebrities, hot posts, cache rebuild stampedes, lag.
  • Seniors connect it to storage choices (sharding by author vs id), cost, and the staged evolution seen in the Chirp scaling track.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only the happy path.
  • Forgetting deletes, blocks and privacy filtering.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Feed = per-user list of post ids. Push (fan-out on write) makes reads cheap; pull makes writes cheap; hybrid uses push for normal authors and pull for celebrities.
  • Numbers: 100k feed reads/s, 350k fan-out inserts/s, about 2 TB of ids in Redis; media goes to CDN.
  • Use Snowflake ids, cursor pagination, ids-only caches, batched hydration, and a rebuild path.
  • Rank in two stages (candidates, model) inside a 200 ms budget, with a chronological fallback.
  • Hot counters need sharded or async counting; deletes are tombstones filtered at hydration.
  • Fan-out through Kafka and workers; protect against lag and stampedes.

questions.promptHtml: Explain fan-out on write versus fan-out on read for a home feed, and which you would pick.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the central decision of the problem; the answer must include the celebrity case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Push: when someone posts, insert the post id into every follower's feed list, so a read is one cache call but a write costs as many inserts as followers. Pull: on read, fetch recent posts from each followee and merge: cheap writes, expensive reads. I pick hybrid: push for normal authors, pull for authors above a follower threshold, merging their recent posts at read time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
With 300M DAU, 150M posts/day and 200 average followers, push is 30B inserts/day, about 350k/s: fine across a Redis cluster. A celebrity post with 100M followers means 100M inserts for one post: a storm. Pull for everyone means 200 lookups per feed open at 100k opens/s, 20M lookups/s.

Reader -> Feed service -> pushed feed (Redis) + celebrity timelines (cache) -> merge -> page

Extras: skip fan-out for users inactive 30 days (rebuild lazily), prioritise active recipients, keep ids sortable by time so merging is cheap.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def home_feed(user, cursor, n=20):
    ids = redis.zrevrangebyscore(f"feed:{user}", cursor, "-inf", start=0, num=n+20)
    for c in celebrity_followees(user):
        ids += timeline_cache.recent(c, since=cursor, limit=n)
    return hydrate(sorted(set(ids), reverse=True)[:n])

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Push" with no celebrity answer, or "pull" with no read-cost answer.
  • No stated threshold.
  • Merging without time-sorted ids.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How choose the threshold? -> Follower count (100k to 1M) tuned by fan-out cost and lag; per-author policy knob.
  2. User follows many celebrities? -> Cap or rank which ones to pull.
  3. When is pure pull right? -> Ranked feeds computed per request anyway.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: picks push. Senior: hybrid with numbers, inactive-user skipping, lag fallback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A celebrity post once backed up fan-out workers for hours, delaying everyone's posts.

questions.promptHtml: Why should a feed use cursor pagination with Snowflake-style ids rather than page numbers or OFFSET?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks API design under a moving dataset.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: New posts keep arriving at the top, so offsets shift and the user sees duplicates or misses items. A cursor says "continue after this post id". Snowflake ids embed a timestamp in the high bits, so id order is time order, ids are generated without coordination, and the same id serves as cursor and as the sort key in the Redis feed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Layout: 41 bits time, 10 bits machine, 12 bits sequence (Twitter's scheme). GET /feed/home?cursor=<id>&limit=20 returns items with id < cursor and nextCursor. Backed by ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 (cursor -inf LIMIT 0 20 or WHERE post_id < :cursor ORDER BY post_id DESC LIMIT 20. OFFSET also costs O(offset) in SQL.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• OFFSET pagination.
  • Opaque cursors that cannot be resumed after a feed rebuild.
  • Trusting client clocks for ordering.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Ranked feed cursor? -> Cursor encodes the ranker session snapshot or last score position; ranked pages cached 30 to 60 s.
  2. Clock skew between generators? -> Roughly ordered; fine for feeds, not for money.
  3. How to refresh the top? -> Ask since=<newest id> separately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "cursor is better". Senior: explains the id structure, SQL and Redis forms, ranked-cursor complication.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An offset-based timeline showed duplicate tweets while users scrolled during a busy event.

questions.contextHtml: A celebrity with 80M followers posts at 20:00. By 20:03 normal users report their own posts take 6 minutes to appear for followers. Metrics: fan-out Kafka consumer lag 900M, fan-out workers CPU 85%, Redis cluster CPU 55%, post service latency normal, social graph read p99 up from 8 ms to 140 ms. The team notices Redis memory growth 2% and suggests adding Redis nodes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds Redis nodes (red herring); never questions pushing 80M inserts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a celebrity threshold? Does the lag affect only this author's topic partition or everyone's? Is graph reading followers in pages?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop pushing this author's post: flag them as pull-only, skip their pending fan-out messages, and let readers merge the post at read time. Reprioritise workers to drain normal-author partitions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: One author's job dominates shared workers; follower-list fetch is the hot path (graph p99 up); too few partitions keyed by author put all the work on one worker.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-partition lag, worker thread dumps, graph QPS by key, fan-out inserts per second.
  5. Root cause: Write amplification equals follower count: 80M inserts for one post, sharing workers with ordinary traffic.
  6. Fix: Hybrid with a threshold (for example above 1M followers: no push); cache celebrity timelines for 1 to 5 s locally; keep celebrity posts in their own cached timeline; separate topics for high-follower authors; active-user-only fan-out.
  7. Prevention: Alert on fan-out lag seconds and per-author fan-out size; load test with a synthetic 100M post.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pull adds read cost (merge up to ~20 celebrities per user); reversible per author. I would not buy hardware to run an unbounded loop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Follower threshold wrong? -> A per-author policy knob, adjusted from lag data.
  • Fan-out lags anyway? -> Posts stay visible via the author's timeline; the feed is slightly stale, not empty.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An unreleased-album announcement from an account just under the threshold pushed 900k inserts per second for ten minutes; lowering the threshold moved it to pull permanently.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale Redis.
  • Hire: hybrid, treat author as pull.
  • Strong hire: separate partitions, inactive skipping, metrics and per-author policy.

questions.contextHtml: Users complain that a deleted post keeps appearing, and a blocked user's posts still show for 2 hours. Each feed entry in Redis is stored as the full post JSON (about 1.2 KB) pushed at write time. The delete flow calls DELETE FROM posts WHERE id=? only. At 800 entries for 300M users that would be roughly 290 TB, so only a fraction of users are cached and the rest are rebuilt.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what is the corrected design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run a job to scan all feeds and remove it": 300M lists, forever.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is edit support needed? Is GDPR hard delete required? How fast must blocking take effect?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Filter at read time with a tombstone list and a block-list lookup in the feed service.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Bodies copied into feeds (storage, edits, deletes impossible), no tombstone, no read-time privacy filter.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check feed entry size and a sample of post ids against the posts table.
  5. Root cause: The feed is a copy, not a pointer; truth is duplicated 200x.
  6. Fix: Store ids only (8 B x 800 x 300M is about 2 TB), hydrate from the posts cache in batched MGET, soft delete (tombstone), hydrator drops tombstoned posts instantly; publish post.deleted so workers clean feeds lazily; apply block/mute filter at read time too; GDPR hard delete as an async job.
  7. Prevention: Test: delete then read feed in the same second must not show it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Hydration adds an extra batched read (about 20 ms) but makes edits, deletes and privacy correct. I would not rely on cleaning every feed synchronously.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ghost ids make a page short? -> Over-fetch (n+20) and top up.
  • Private account toggled? -> Same read-time filter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A takedown for legal reasons took six hours to propagate through copied feed bodies; ids-only plus tombstones made it immediate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scan all feeds.
  • Hire: ids only, hydrate, tombstone.
  • Strong hire: read-time block filter, lazy cleanup, over-fetch, GDPR flow.

questions.contextHtml: A startup CTO says: "We need a news feed for our fitness app. We have 2M registered users, maybe 150k DAU, people follow about 40 others, 30k posts a day. Design it like Twitter." Team size is 5 engineers on Postgres and Redis.
questions.promptHtml: What do you design, and what do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Draws the full Twitter hybrid with Kafka fan-out workers and a feature store.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Chronological or ranked? Do any accounts have many thousands of followers? Latency target? Are posts editable or deletable? Expected growth next year?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a; frame it as right-sizing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Numbers: 150k DAU x 10 opens/day = 1.5M reads/day (about 17/s avg, peak maybe 100/s); 30k posts/day x 40 followers = 1.2M inserts/day (14/s). That is tiny.
  4. How I'd verify each: Back-of-envelope in the room; confirm no celebrity skew.
  5. Root cause: n/a.
  6. Fix (proposal): Fan-out on read with a good index: SELECT ... FROM posts WHERE author_id IN (followees) ORDER BY post_id DESC LIMIT 20, cached in Redis for 30 s. Snowflake-style ids, cursor pagination, a follows table with an index each way. Plan the upgrade path: when one account crosses thousands of followers or reads exceed Postgres capacity, add push for normal authors, keeping the API unchanged.
  7. Prevention: Metrics: feed p99, query time, followers per author; thresholds to trigger the next stage.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build Kafka fan-out, ranking and a feature store for 100 req/s; complexity is a cost the five-person team pays daily.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• They want ranking? -> Start with a simple score (recency x engagement) in SQL or in app; ML later.
  • Growth to 10M DAU? -> Staged evolution as in the Chirp scaling track: cache, then push, then hybrid.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A small team shipped a distributed fan-out system for a few thousand users and then spent months operating it; the monolithic query with a cache would have lasted two more years.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: over-engineers.
  • Hire: asks and picks pull with cache.
  • Strong hire: numbers, upgrade triggers, API stability.

questions.contextHtml: At 09:00 one Redis shard (holding feeds for 10M users) crashes; the replica was also being resynced after a maintenance restart. Feed service error rate hits 30% and p99 rises from 120 ms to 6 s. The rebuild path (followees + recent posts from the Posts DB) runs per user on a cache miss. Posts DB CPU 95%, connection pool exhausted, graph service latency 10x. 800k users per minute are opening the app.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restarts the feed service repeatedly and waits.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the feed cache derived and rebuildable (yes)? Is there a stale fallback? Does rebuild coalesce requests?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed and throttle: rate-limit rebuilds (token bucket), serve a degraded feed (recent posts from top followees or a generic popular feed) instead of an empty one, enable request coalescing per user, shorten the page size.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cache stampede on rebuild; connection pool exhaustion from long rebuild queries; graph service overloaded by 200 lookups per user.
  4. How I'd verify each: DB active connections, rebuild count per second, cache hit ratio, per-shard error rate.
  5. Root cause: Losing one shard converted 10M cached reads into 10M simultaneous expensive rebuilds against a shared DB.
  6. Fix: Throttle with jitter, coalesce concurrent rebuilds, prewarm active users first, limit rebuild to the latest 200 posts and extend lazily, keep the replica healthy (never restart replica and primary together), a stale-while-revalidate tier.
  7. Prevention: Load test shard loss monthly; alert on rebuild QPS; budget DB capacity for 10% concurrent rebuild.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Degraded feeds hurt engagement briefly; an overloaded DB hurts everything. I would not pay for strong durability on a derived cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rebuild takes 500 ms each? -> That is why only active users rebuild eagerly; others on return.
  • Consistent hashing vs Redis Cluster slots? -> Either; the point is bounded blast radius per shard.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a cache flush at 08:55 the product was effectively down until a rebuild limiter was added; later flushes were invisible.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits or restarts.
  • Hire: throttle, degrade, coalesce.
  • Strong hire: blast-radius reasoning, prewarm active users, game days.

questions.contextHtml:
A post goes viral at 120k likes/s. The like handler is:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO likes(user_id, post_id) VALUES ($1,$2);
UPDATE posts SET like_count = like_count + 1 WHERE post_id = $2;
COMMIT;

Symptoms: Postgres shows 3,000 sessions waiting on transactionid/tuple locks, like API p99 22 s, other writes to posts (new posts, edits) on the same shard time out. CPU on the DB is only 30%. Users double-tapping sometimes see +2.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what is the corrected design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds an index or a bigger instance (CPU is not the bottleneck).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is an exact public count required? Can the like be asynchronous? Is (user, post) unique?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable inline count updates for hot posts; show a cached or approximate count; queue likes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Row-lock contention on a single hot row, serialised commits; missing uniqueness permits double count; hot shard blocks unrelated writes.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_activity wait events, pg_locks, row-level lock waits, unique constraint check.
  5. Root cause: Every like serialises on the same row, throughput is bounded by one row's lock, not CPU.
  6. Fix: Write the like event (user, post) to Kafka and a likes table with a unique key (user_id, post_id) for idempotence. Count in Redis with INCR, sharded for hot keys (N sub-counters, sum on read), flushed periodically to the DB. Public count approximate; "did I like it" exact from the likes store.
  7. Prevention: Load test one-key hot spots; alert on lock waits; contract: counts are eventually consistent.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Approximate counts are a product decision that removes the hottest row in the system; reversible. I would not use a single row counter at scale.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Unlike? -> A compensating event, with the unique key still enforcing idempotence.
  • Count shown differs between users? -> Accept seconds of skew; converge on flush.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single viral post held the whole posts shard hostage for 25 minutes; sub-counters removed the contention entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bigger DB.
  • Hire: async counters plus unique like key.
  • Strong hire: sharded sub-counters, exactness split, hot-shard isolation.

questions.contextHtml: After launching a ranked feed, feed p99 rose from 180 ms to 780 ms, SLO 200 ms. Trace breakdown for p99: Redis candidates 6 ms, post hydration 190 ms (cache hit ratio 62%, misses fetch posts one by one), feature fetch 210 ms (per-candidate calls for 500 candidates), model scoring 300 ms (CPU model server at 90% CPU). The ranker is called synchronously and has no fallback.
questions.promptHtml: Bring it back under budget and make it safe.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds caches randomly or removes ranking.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a stale ranked page acceptable? Can we reduce candidates? What is the business impact of ranking vs chronological?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill switch to chronological ordering (the fallback), reduce candidates from 500 to 200.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N+1 hydration misses, per-candidate feature calls, undersized or unbatched model serving.
  4. How I'd verify each: Distributed traces, cache hit ratio, batching size in the model server, GPU/CPU utilisation.
  5. Root cause: Per-item calls instead of batches, low cache hit rate, no latency budget enforcement.
  6. Fix: Budget: ids 5 ms, hydrate 20 ms (batched MGET, one WHERE post_id IN (...) for misses, target 95% hit), features 30 ms (batched from a feature store with precomputed affinity), model 50 ms (batched inference, smaller model, autoscale), counters 10 ms. Cache the final ranked page 30 to 60 s per user to survive refresh spam. Timeouts per stage with graceful degradation.
  7. Prevention: Per-stage latency alerts; A/B launch gates on p99; kill switch drills.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Ranking is reversible policy but costs infra; I would not wait on the ranker without a timeout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ranker times out? -> Return chronological candidates with a header flag.
  • Filter bubble concerns? -> Diversity rules and a chronological tab.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Cutting candidates from 500 to 150 lost almost no engagement and halved model cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random caching.
  • Hire: batching and fallback.
  • Strong hire: stage budgets, timeouts, page caching, candidate sizing trade-off.
